title: Why Men Never Move On.
subtitle: A scientific investigation into male heartbreak, questionable emotional support systems, divorced-dad behaviour, and why some of my friends are still fighting wars that ended years ago.
excerpt: Why do some men look perfectly fine after a breakup, only to spend the next three years listening to the same five songs, remembering conversations from 2022, and behaving like divorced fathers whose children visit every alternate weekend? Let’s look at the science, the jokes, and the rather unfortunate possibility that moving on is not as simple as we pretend.

content.lead: There are two kinds of men after a breakup. The first becomes a 'divorced dad' in spirit: emotionally unavailable, suspiciously quiet, and somehow still remembering the exact date of a conversation from three years ago. The second becomes a 'playboy', collecting new names, new faces, and new situationships like achievements on a video game. They look like opposites. But I have a theory that both might be searching for the same person.

sections.heading: First of All, This Is a Public Service Announcement for My Friends.
paragraphs: If you are reading this and immediately thought, “He is definitely talking about me,” congratulations. Self-awareness is the first step. The second step is deleting that old chat, and the third is perhaps finally returning to the group chat instead of disappearing every time her name comes up.
I am kidding. Mostly.

We have all seen it. Someone gets their heart broken and suddenly develops the personality of a retired man who spends his evenings staring at the sea. Another friend starts entertaining every girl who gives him the slightest bit of attention. And then there is the friend who claims he has moved on but can somehow provide a detailed historical account of his ex’s Instagram activity.
The breakup happened years ago. The investigation is apparently still ongoing.

But jokes aside, why does this happen? Why do some people seem to recover while others carry a relationship around long after it has ended? And is there any truth to the idea that men never really move on?

sections.heading: The Science: Do Men Actually Hurt More?
paragraphs: Let us start with a little reality check. A 2015 study by Craig Morris, Elizabeth Reiber, and colleagues surveyed 5,705 people across 96 countries about their experiences after romantic breakups. Women reported greater emotional anguish on average, scoring 6.84 out of 10 compared with 6.58 for men. They also reported greater physical pain.

That does not mean women love more, or that men care less. It tells us something more useful: heartbreak hurts both, but people can experience and express it differently. The study was based on people recalling past breakups, so it cannot tell us exactly how quickly each gender recovers.

Another study, published in PNAS in 2022, found that people who initiated a separation generally experienced better subjective well-being than those who did not. It makes intuitive sense. If you have spent months accepting that a relationship is ending, you may have begun grieving before the other person even realises what is happening.
Imagine being the person who still thinks you are building a future together, only to discover that the other person has already started imagining a life without you.
That is not simply losing someone. It is finding out that the future you were preparing for may have existed in your head more completely than it ever existed between you.
Sources: [Morris et al., 2015, Social Psychological and Personality Science](https://doi.org/10.1037/ebs0000054) and [PNAS, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9191343/).

sections.heading: Men Are Not Always Great at Asking for Help.
paragraphs: Here is where things get interesting. A Pew Research Center survey of 6,204 US adults, published in January 2025, found that women were more likely than men to turn to friends, parents, other family members, and mental health professionals for emotional support.
For example, 54% of women said they would turn to a friend for emotional support, compared with 38% of men. Women were also more likely to turn to their mothers and other family members.

These are US findings, not universal statistics about every man on the planet. But they raise a fair question: if you have been taught to keep your feelings to yourself, where exactly are those feelings supposed to go when your relationship falls apart?
Some men have friends they can tell absolutely anything. Others have friends with whom the deepest conversation ever attempted is, “Bhai, kya scene hai?” followed by a meme and a change of subject.

And so the feelings remain. Sometimes they become silence. Sometimes anger. Sometimes work, gym sessions, jokes, rebounds, or an alarming interest in becoming the most emotionally unavailable man alive.

A relationship can become more than romance when it is also the only place a person feels genuinely understood. Losing that person can mean losing a partner, a confidant, a routine, and the one place where you felt comfortable being vulnerable.
That is a lot to lose at once.
Source: [Pew Research Center, Men, Women and Social Connections, 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2025/01/16/men-women-and-social-connections/).

sections.heading: The Divorced Dad and the Playboy Are Looking for the Same Person.
paragraphs: Now, back to my highly scientific theory.

After a breakup, one man decides that love is a scam. He becomes quiet, stops making plans, and acts as though his greatest ambition is to sit in a chair and watch the world pass him by. He is not necessarily sad every second. He may genuinely enjoy his peace. But somewhere along the way, he has stopped expecting anyone to understand him the way she did.
We shall call him the divorced dad.

Then there is the other man. He starts going out more, meeting new people, flirting, dating, and insisting that he is having the time of his life. Every new girl is another chance to feel something again. He may even convince himself that he has finally escaped the past.
We shall call him the playboy.
One has stopped searching. The other has never stopped.

But what if both are trying to find the same feeling? The comfort of being understood without having to explain every little thing. The familiarity of a voice. The stupid inside jokes. The person you wanted to tell when something wonderful happened, or when the entire day went horribly wrong.

Maybe the divorced dad has accepted that he may never find it again. Maybe the playboy keeps searching for it in every new person he meets. Neither possibility means every man behaves this way, of course. People heal differently, and some move forward without carrying their past into every new relationship.

But for those who do struggle, perhaps the saddest part is not that they keep looking for her. It is that, without realising it, they may start looking for her in people who never had a chance to be themselves.

They meet someone new and compare her laugh, her kindness, her habits, her way of speaking. They look for familiar feelings in an unfamiliar person. And when the new person turns out to be different, as a whole human being inevitably will, they wonder why it does not feel the same.
Of course it does not. She is not the same person. Neither are you.

sections.heading: The Smell of the First Rain.
paragraphs: There is a saying, or perhaps just a thought I have never been able to phrase properly: the smell of the first rain never feels quite the same twice.

You can stand in the same place, feel the same drops against your skin, and breathe in that familiar smell of wet earth. But something has changed. Maybe it is the year you have lived through. Maybe it is the person who once stood beside you. Maybe it is simply the fact that you cannot experience a moment for the first time twice.
I think people sometimes chase that first rain.

They want to feel that first conversation again. That first notification that made them smile at their phone like an idiot. That first time someone remembered a tiny detail about them. That moment when an ordinary person somehow became the person they wanted to tell everything to.
And the thing about falling in love is that you can begin imagining an entire future with someone before either of you has properly figured out the present.

You picture the little things. The places you will visit. The arguments you will laugh about later. The home you might share. The version of yourself you will become together. You might never say any of it out loud, but somewhere inside your head, the future has already started taking shape.

Then the relationship ends, and it can feel like betrayal. Not always because the other person deliberately betrayed you, but because the future you trusted in has disappeared. You are left grieving conversations that never happened, places you never visited together, and a life that existed so vividly in your imagination that losing it feels almost like losing a real memory.
And perhaps that is why some people struggle to move on. They are not only missing the person. They are missing the person they thought they would become beside them.

But no person can promise to remain exactly who we imagined them to be. Love is not a contract signed by two people agreeing to become the characters in each other’s dreams. The other person is allowed to change. So are we. Sometimes two people can love each other and still arrive at different futures.
That does not make what they shared meaningless. It just makes it painfully human.

sections.heading: The Loyalty Argument. Oh, Here We Go.
paragraphs: Whenever people discuss heartbreak, somebody eventually declares that men are more loyal, women move on faster, or one gender loves more deeply than the other. It is a satisfying argument because it gives pain a scoreboard. If I am hurting more, surely I must have loved more. If you moved on first, surely you never cared.

But the research does not give us a clean winner. A 2026 study examining romantic relationship closure found that factors such as initiating the breakup, time since the breakup, and entering a new relationship were associated with greater closure. Continued contact-seeking and attachment anxiety were associated with less closure. However, men made up only 12.1% of that study’s sample, so its gender findings should be interpreted cautiously.

Research on divorce also suggests that the aftermath can differ by gender and life circumstances. One longitudinal study found that men could be more vulnerable to short-term declines in subjective well-being after divorce, while women were more likely to face persistent economic hardship. These are different kinds of pain, and neither cancels out the other.

So no, we cannot honestly conclude that men are inherently more loyal or that women simply move on because they care less. We can say that people have different support systems, different circumstances, and different ways of processing loss.
And we should probably stop treating someone’s recovery as evidence that their love was fake.

Sources: [2026 study on relationship closure](https://doi.org/10.1080/09515070.2026.2666640), [longitudinal study on separation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39418415/), and [Leopold, 2018, on divorce and well-being](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5992251/).

sections.heading: So, What Are We Actually Praying For?
paragraphs: There is another part of heartbreak that is difficult to explain without sounding a little dramatic. And I am perfectly willing to sound dramatic for a few paragraphs. You have made it this far, so please bear with me.

Sometimes you pray for someone. Not necessarily in some grand, cinematic way. Maybe you simply ask God to let things work out. You hope that the person you care about will stay, that the future you have imagined will somehow become real, that all the little signs you have been holding on to will eventually make sense.
And then it does not happen.
What are you supposed to do with that?

How do you keep praying when the very thing you prayed for is the thing you have to learn to live without? What is the point of asking God for something with your whole heart if you eventually have to accept that it may never be yours?

I do not have a neat answer. I do not want to pretend that every heartbreak happens for a beautiful reason or that the universe has some perfectly timed replacement waiting around the corner. Sometimes people leave. Sometimes things do not work out. Sometimes you can do everything you know how to do and still lose something you desperately wanted to keep.

Maybe faith is not a guarantee that we will receive everything we ask for. Maybe it is the difficult, sometimes frustrating belief that our lives can still hold meaning when the answer is not what we hoped for.

And maybe moving on is not about convincing yourself that you never needed that person. It is about accepting that loving someone deeply does not give you ownership over the rest of their life, or a guarantee that they will remain part of yours.

You can miss someone and still wish them well. You can be grateful for what happened without pretending the ending did not hurt. You can keep the memory without making it responsible for every decision you make next.
I know. Easier to write than to practise. Trust me, I am aware.

sections.heading: To My Friends Who Are Still Fighting the War.
paragraphs: This is where I stop pretending I am conducting an entirely objective investigation into the emotional behaviour of men.

To my friends who are still holding on to someone who left years ago: I hope you find peace. Not because she did not matter, and not because you should be embarrassed about caring. I hope you find peace because you deserve a life that is bigger than the worst thing that happened to your heart.

You do not have to hate her to move on. You do not have to pretend she was terrible, rewrite every good memory, or convince yourself that the relationship meant nothing. You can acknowledge that she mattered and still accept that the chapter is over.

And if you are the friend who has turned into a playboy, please remember that the women you meet now are not auditions for the role of your ex. Let them be people, not comparisons. Someone new deserves to be known for who she is, not measured against the ghost of somebody else.
Aayush, if you are reading this, sorry for the trouble, man. I genuinely hope you have moved on. Just like me, obviously. Haha :)
And to the rest of you: please stop sending me the same sad song at 2 AM and then claiming you are doing fantastic. I love you, but the evidence is not in your favour.

sections.heading: A Note to Her. Maybe.
paragraphs: I do not know if this belongs here, but perhaps that is the point of having a personal archive. Not everything needs to arrive at a perfectly organised conclusion.

Maybe a part of me still remembers the future I once imagined. Maybe writing about love, heartbreak, and people who struggle to let go is a way of understanding things I could never explain properly when they were happening.
Or maybe I just enjoy writing dramatic articles about my friends. We may never know.

There is a meme about Stan Lee creating an entire cinematic universe for one girl. I know it is a joke, not a historical explanation of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but I understand the feeling behind it. Sometimes a person becomes so significant that they leave traces in the things you make, the stories you love, and the way you see the world afterward.
Superhero stories have always understood something about love and loss: saving the world does not necessarily mean you get to keep the person you wanted to save it for.

And maybe that is what makes those stories hurt. The hero can fight impossible villains, survive the end of the world, and do things no ordinary person could dream of doing. But there are some things even a hero cannot force to work out.

If any of this reminds me of you, perhaps that is simply because you were part of my life. I do not need to turn that into a grand declaration, and I do not need to pretend the memories never mattered.
Some people leave, but the time we spent with them remains part of the person we become. I think I can live with that.

sections.heading: So, Have I Moved On?
paragraphs: I think I have. I really do.

But perhaps moving on is not the same as forgetting. Maybe it is being able to remember without needing the past to change. Maybe it is accepting that the smell of the first rain will never be exactly the same twice, and deciding to step outside anyway when it rains again.

Maybe one day someone will make me laugh in a way I have never laughed before. Maybe I will discover new places, build a different future, and find that life still has surprises left for me. And maybe, when that happens, I will not compare any of it to what came before.
I do not know. I am twenty, and apparently I have decided to write a research-backed investigation into why half my friends are emotionally retired.
But if there is one thing I hope we take from all this, it is that moving on does not mean the person never mattered. It means their absence no longer gets to decide what your life can become.
You can miss her. You can remember her. You can even admit that a part of you wishes things had gone differently.
Just do not spend the rest of your life waiting for the first rain to smell the same.
Anyway, that was disgustingly sincere.
Lmao.

8. Harvard Health Publishing. Discussion of marriage, men’s health, and social support. [Read the article](https://www.health.harvard.edu/mens-health/marriage-and-mens-health).

These studies examine different populations and different outcomes. They do not prove that all men behave alike, that women move on faster in every circumstance, or that one gender is inherently more loyal. The personal theories, jokes, and reflections in this article are my interpretations, not scientific conclusions.

title: Nobody Cares About Your Shitty Business.
subtitle: Another business. Another AI agent. Another CEO on LinkedIn. At what point do we stop trying to look like entrepreneurs and actually build something worth caring about?
excerpt: Another clothing brand. Another jewellery store. Another AI agent that promises to revolutionise your workflow. And another LinkedIn bio announcing a CEO who may be running a company of three people. I do not want you to fail. I just want to know what exactly you are building, why it matters, and whether there is anything beneath the title.

content.lead: Nobody cares about your shitty business. And before you start typing an angry paragraph about how I am jealous, bitter, or some engineering student who should mind his own business, relax. I am getting there. Because this is not just about you. It is about my friends, the startup culture around me, the LinkedIn profiles I keep coming across, my own ambitions, and a question I think we should all be asking ourselves a little more often.

sections.heading: First of all, good luck. Seriously.
paragraphs: Let me start with something that might surprise you. I do not promote my friends’ businesses.

Not because I secretly want them to fail. Not because I am jealous that someone my age is making money while I am sitting in front of my laptop trying to figure out what on earth I am doing with my life. And certainly not because I think I am better than them.
I just do not really do that. The least I can do is wish them luck, and that is what I actually do.
Someone starts a clothing brand? Good luck, bro. Someone starts selling jewellery? All the best. Someone launches a new Instagram page for their business? Nice. I hope it works out for you.
And I mean it.

Because at least they started something. They had an idea, decided to do something about it, and took the first step. That already puts them ahead of the version of themselves who would have spent another six months talking about it without doing anything.
Meanwhile, what exactly am I doing? Lmao.

Who am I to sit on my high horse and judge someone for trying to make something work? Am I a millionaire already? Have I built a company that employs hundreds of people? Have I solved some massive problem that humanity has been struggling with for centuries?

No. I am a twenty-year-old engineering student with a bunch of ideas, a laptop, unfinished projects, and an unreasonable amount of ambition. My bank account is not exactly in a position to deliver keynote speeches about entrepreneurship.
So, no, I am not going to laugh at someone simply because they decided to start a business. I know how vulnerable it can feel to put something you made into the world and wait for people to react.
I know what it feels like to be excited about an idea and have someone dismiss it before they have even understood what you are trying to do.
Which is precisely why I want to talk about this.

sections.heading: But seriously, another clothing brand?
paragraphs: Another clothing brand. Another jewellery store. Another Instagram page reselling clothes. Another business announcement with a carefully designed logo, a few product photographs, and a caption about beginning an exciting entrepreneurial journey.
And suddenly, everyone is an entrepreneur.

Now, before someone misunderstands me, there is absolutely nothing wrong with selling clothes. There is nothing wrong with jewellery. There is nothing wrong with reselling products, building a small shop, or starting a business that already has competitors.

Not every business needs to reinvent capitalism. Not everyone wants to build the next Google. A small business can support a family, give someone financial independence, provide a useful service, or simply help a person earn their first income. Those are perfectly legitimate reasons to start something.

And yes, established businesses can still leave room for better pricing, better quality, better customer service, better design, or a more focused audience. A familiar category does not automatically mean a pointless business.
But I want you to think about what you have actually started.

What is new about it? What problem are you solving? Who is struggling with that problem? Why would they choose you over the hundreds of people already selling similar things? What makes your product, service, experience, or approach meaningfully different?

And if your answer is that your products are good quality, your prices are affordable, or your designs are unique, that is a starting point. But can you explain what makes those claims true? Can you show people? Can you deliver consistently? Can you give them a reason to return?
You do not necessarily need an original idea. You need a reason for your business to exist beyond the fact that you wanted to start one.

There is a difference between opening a business and building a business. The first can happen in an afternoon. The second demands that you keep answering difficult questions long after the excitement of launching has worn off.

A logo is not a business strategy. An Instagram page is not proof of demand. A launch announcement is not product-market fit. And having your friends congratulate you is not the same as having customers who genuinely need what you offer.
You can start with a simple idea. Absolutely. But at some point, you need to look beyond the fact that you started.

And honestly, this is not just about clothing brands or jewellery stores anymore. The same question applies to the entire startup ecosystem, especially the one that has discovered artificial intelligence and apparently decided that every existing business model needs to be wrapped in an AI-powered subscription.
Because if there is one thing I have noticed lately, it is that the word “AI” can make an ordinary product sound extraordinary before anyone has even explained what the product does.

sections.heading: Is your aim just to make money?
paragraphs: Here is where I might lose some people.
Is your only goal to make money?
And before you tell me that making money is literally the point of a business, yes. I know. Thank you for the economics lesson. I have not forgotten how the world works.

There is nothing shameful about wanting financial independence. Money pays bills, feeds families, creates choices, and gives people room to breathe. I would never tell someone that they should feel guilty for wanting to earn more of it.
But surely there is more to building something than announcing that you are now a business owner.

What do you want your business to become? What do you want to improve? What would make you proud of the thing you are building five years from now? If someone else can provide the exact same thing, in the exact same way, to the exact same customers, what is the reason your business should survive?

Maybe your answer is that you want to create employment. Maybe you want to make something more accessible. Maybe you have noticed that an existing service treats customers badly and you believe you can do better. Maybe you have discovered a group of people whose needs are being ignored.

Or maybe you simply love fashion and want to build a clothing brand. That is fine too. Your personal taste, creative direction, community, or understanding of a particular audience can become the foundation of something meaningful.
But know what you are trying to build.
Do not confuse the feeling of being an entrepreneur with the work of becoming one. Do not fall in love with the title so much that you forget to examine the actual business.
And please, do not start something solely because entrepreneurship looks cool on LinkedIn.
Actually, can we talk about LinkedIn for a second?
Have you seen some of these bios already?
CEO of this. CMO of that. CTO of something else. Founder and visionary. Serial entrepreneur. Building the future of whatever happens to be trending this week.
And sometimes I look at these profiles and think, mate, what are we doing? 😭

CEO of what, exactly? A company with a website, three people in a WhatsApp group, and a product that has not left the prototype stage? CMO of what marketing department? Who are you marketing to? Your other two co-founders?
And look, I KNOW. Before someone starts writing a LinkedIn post about how disrespectful this is, let me explain myself.

There is nothing wrong with being the CEO of a small company. There is nothing wrong with being a founder before you have employees, revenue, or a fancy office. Every real company has to begin somewhere. If you have taken responsibility for building something, you are allowed to say so.
The problem is not the title. The problem is when the title becomes the product.

When you spend more time presenting yourself as a founder than actually building the company you founded, something has gone horribly wrong. When your most impressive achievement is the designation written underneath your name, I have to wonder what exactly you are trying to prove.

Does having CEO in your bio make you a better entrepreneur? Does putting CMO beside your name magically give you a marketing strategy? Does calling yourself a CTO mean you have built technology worth using?
Or did you just want the title because it sounds cool?
Seriously. What is the obsession?
Is it money? Is it fame? Is it the attention? Is it the little rush you get when someone visits your profile, sees “Founder & CEO,” and assumes you must be doing something extraordinary?
Did you get all the attention you needed? Do you feel important now? Lmao.
JUST FUCK YOU GUYS ALREADY.
Okay, maybe that was a little aggressive. But genuinely, what are we doing?

We have somehow turned entrepreneurship into an identity badge. Everyone wants to be a founder. Everyone wants to be a CEO. Everyone wants to announce that they are building something disruptive, innovative, revolutionary, and completely unlike anything the world has ever seen.
And then you click the website, and it is another landing page with three gradients, a waitlist form, and the words “the future of productivity.”
BRO. PLEASE.
Where is the product? Where are the users? What have you learned? What problem did you actually solve? What did you build that did not exist before, or what did you make meaningfully better?

I would be far more impressed by someone who quietly builds a genuinely useful product, gets ten customers who love it, listens to their complaints, fixes what is broken, and slowly grows than someone who announces themselves as the CEO of the next billion-dollar company before they have figured out what their first customer needs.

And no, revenue is not the only measure of whether something matters. Early-stage projects need time. Open-source tools can create enormous value without generating much money. Social enterprises can measure success in ways that go beyond profit. A student project can be worth building simply because of what its creators learn.
But there should be something real beneath the presentation. Some work. Some learning. Some evidence that you are trying to do more than look impressive.
Your LinkedIn bio should describe what you are doing. It should not be a substitute for doing it.
You do not become a founder because you have found the correct combination of words to put underneath your name. You become one by taking responsibility for something you are trying to build.

And you do not need to look successful every second of the process. You are allowed to be a beginner. You are allowed to have no idea what you are doing yet. You are allowed to build something small without pretending it is going to change the world.
Honestly, that would be refreshing.

sections.heading: The AI startup scene is a whole different level of comedy.
paragraphs: Now, let us get to the part that really makes me question everything.
Artificial intelligence.

Every other day, there is another AI startup announcing some revolutionary agent. An AI assistant that manages your tasks. An AI agent that browses the internet for you. An AI agent that writes your emails, organises your calendar, researches your competitors, automates your workflow, and probably makes you breakfast if you write the prompt correctly.
Everything is AI-powered. Everything is autonomous. Everything is revolutionary. Everything is going to change the world.
And sometimes I look at these products and genuinely wonder: what exactly are we doing here?
You took an existing AI model, connected it to a few tools, wrapped it in an interface, added a subscription page, and called it the future of work.
Congratulations. You have discovered that APIs exist.

Okay, that is obviously an exaggeration. Building a reliable product involves much more than connecting an API to a button. There is engineering, evaluation, security, user experience, reliability, and an enormous amount of work that nobody sees. I know that.

Using existing models is not cheating. You do not need to train a foundation model from scratch to build something useful. Some of the best products will come from people who understand a particular industry, know its problems, and use existing technology to solve them better.
But you know what I am getting at.
If your entire business depends on a feature that a much larger AI company can build directly into its existing product, what exactly protects you?

Imagine building your entire startup around the idea of an AI agent that works in the background, remembers what matters to you, connects to your applications, and completes tasks on your behalf. You spend months building the product, raising money, designing the branding, and explaining to investors why your agent is the future.
Then OpenAI announces dots.

On 29 September 2026, OpenAI introduced dots, its always-on AI agents designed to work towards user goals, use their own cloud computers, connect with thousands of apps, and make progress on tasks between conversations. The announcement describes them as agents that can take on ongoing responsibilities and help people get work done. You can read the announcement here: https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/
Now, imagine you are a startup whose entire pitch is essentially that.

I am not saying OpenAI has killed every AI agent startup. That would be stupid. Dots is not automatically better than every specialised product, and a product announcement is not proof that every capability works perfectly in every real-world situation.
But you should probably be asking some uncomfortable questions.

If a company with powerful models, existing users, substantial infrastructure, and an ecosystem of integrations can offer a similar capability, why should customers choose you? What happens when the underlying model becomes better? What happens when the feature you spent a year building becomes a standard feature in a product people already use?
And if your answer is simply that your interface looks nicer, your prompts are better, or your agent can do three things that the latest model could not do last month, I have some bad news for you.
Your advantage might have an expiry date.

Today, your startup has an AI agent. Tomorrow, the model provider introduces a similar feature. Another company offers it for less. Eventually, users start expecting that capability to come bundled with something they already pay for.
And suddenly, the thing you called your competitive advantage is a checkbox on somebody else’s pricing page.

I cannot help finding that fascinating. We have people being laughed at for proposing ambitious hardware and engineering projects because they are supposedly too difficult to build, while other people can build a thin product around a trending AI capability and announce that they are reinventing an entire industry.

Why is one person’s ambition treated as delusion while another person’s familiar idea becomes a billion-dollar pitch deck? Why are we so impressed by the word “AI” that we sometimes forget to ask the most basic question of all: what does this actually do for anyone?

And I want to be clear: I am not against AI startups. I am excited about what people can build with AI. A specialised agent that understands a complex industry, handles a difficult workflow reliably, integrates deeply with existing systems, protects sensitive data, or delivers measurable results can be incredibly valuable.

A startup does not need to invent a new algorithm every Tuesday. It does not need to create its own foundation model. A business can create value by combining existing technology intelligently, understanding a specific customer, and solving a problem that larger companies have overlooked.
But using AI is not, by itself, a business model. And adding an agent to a product does not automatically make that product innovative.

Where is your differentiation? Is it specialised knowledge that general-purpose tools do not have? Is it access to data that competitors cannot easily reproduce? Is it deep integration into a workflow that customers cannot simply replace with another application? Is it trust, reliability, accountability, distribution, or a measurable improvement in how people work?
Can you explain why customers would keep paying you if a bigger company released a similar feature tomorrow?
If the only thing separating your startup from a competitor is a prompt, a thin interface, and a monthly subscription, perhaps you do not have as much of a moat as your pitch deck suggests.

And if your response is that you will simply add more features, congratulations. You are now in a race against companies that may have more engineers, more money, more users, and direct control over the technology your business depends on.
Good luck. Seriously.

This is the part people should be discussing before they put “AI founder” in their bios. Not whether the demo looks impressive. Not whether the launch post gets a thousand likes. Not whether the product has a fancy name that sounds like something out of a science-fiction movie.
What happens when the novelty disappears?

What happens when the underlying technology improves? What happens when the next model can do in one instruction what your product currently charges people to do through a complicated workflow? What happens when your customer realises they can achieve almost the same result with a tool they already have?
If you have answers to those questions, brilliant. Build the company. Find the customers. Prove the value. I will be genuinely interested to see what you make.
But if you have not even considered those questions, perhaps hold off on calling yourself the CEO of the future of work.
The future has enough problems without another startup pretending that a wrapper is a revolution.

sections.heading: The price of being too ambitious.
paragraphs: This is the part I understand a little too personally.

Whenever I suggest an idea that feels unfamiliar to the people around me, I often get called delusional, mad, or too ambitious. Sometimes the idea is dismissed before I have even explained how I think it could work.
The reaction is almost predictable.
That is too complex. Nobody would use that. You are wasting your time. Why would you even try? Be realistic, Vedant.

And maybe they are right about some things. Maybe I underestimate the difficulty. Maybe I overlook a constraint. Maybe I get carried away imagining what something could become and fail to appreciate what it would take to get there.
I am willing to accept that possibility. I would rather test an assumption and discover I was wrong than spend my life pretending I was right about everything.
But how are you supposed to discover whether an idea can work if the verdict arrives before the experiment?
How can you tell someone that their idea is impossible when you have not examined the problem, the proposed solution, or the constraints they are trying to work around?
There is a strange thing about ambition. People often celebrate it after it becomes successful. Before that, it can look suspiciously like stupidity.

A person who keeps talking about a big idea is called delusional. A person who builds a successful version of it is called visionary. The idea might be exactly the same. The outcome changes the vocabulary people use to describe it.
Of course, not every rejected idea is secretly brilliant. Sometimes an idea is bad. Sometimes the critics are right. Sometimes the person with the grand vision has not done enough homework.
But there is a difference between saying, "I do not think this will work, and here is why," and saying, "This will never work because I cannot imagine it working."
The first is criticism. The second is a limitation being mistaken for a conclusion.
And there is an irony here that I cannot ignore.

Someone can call themselves the CEO of an AI startup because they have launched a product using existing tools, and people will celebrate their ambition. Someone else can propose a complicated engineering project that requires hardware, software, experimentation, and actual physical work, and people will ask why they are wasting their time.
Why?
Is it because one idea is genuinely better than the other? Sometimes, yes. Is it because one person has a stronger business model or has done more research? Absolutely possible.
Or is it because one idea is easier to package, explain, and post about on LinkedIn?

A clean landing page and an impressive title are immediately understandable. A complicated engineering project requires patience. You have to understand the problem, the components, the constraints, and the reason somebody would spend months attempting to make it work.
One looks impressive before it has proved anything. The other might look ridiculous until somebody sees it working.
And I wonder how many potentially useful ideas get abandoned because the people behind them cannot make their work look impressive before they have actually done the work.
I am not asking people to celebrate every ambitious idea. I am asking them to stop confusing presentation with potential and difficulty with impossibility.

sections.heading: Remember AgriDrone?
paragraphs: When I was building my AgriDrone project, I heard the usual objections.
"Oh, Vedant, this idea is too complex."
"It can never be built."
"You are just wasting money."

And honestly, I understand why someone might look at the project and think that. A drone that combines hardware, software, GPS, a camera, and an agricultural spraying system is not exactly the simplest weekend project for an engineering student.

There are components to understand, systems to integrate, limitations to work around, and a hundred ways for things to go wrong. You cannot simply have a big idea, buy a few parts, and expect everything to magically work because you are passionate about it.
But that was never the point.
The point was to try. To understand how the pieces fit together. To take something that sounded complicated and break it into smaller problems that I could actually work on.

I wanted to explore what could be done when software and hardware were brought together to address a real-world problem. I wanted to learn by building something that could not be completed by simply following another tutorial and copying the result.
Maybe the final version would not look exactly like what I imagined. Maybe some features would need to change. Maybe I would discover limitations that forced me to rethink the design.
That is engineering. You do not get to skip reality just because your idea is exciting. You work with reality until you find something that works.
And if I had listened to every person who told me it was too complex before I even began, I would have learned absolutely nothing about building it.
Even an unsuccessful attempt can teach you something that a hundred hours of imagining cannot.
I am not bringing up AgriDrone to claim that I have revolutionised agriculture. I am not pretending that having a difficult project automatically makes it an important one. It does not.
I bring it up because it reminds me of how quickly people can confuse something being difficult with something being impossible.
Those are not the same thing.

And I want to apply that same standard to myself. If somebody tells me AgriDrone has a technical limitation, I should listen. If somebody points out that a particular design will not work, I should investigate it. If the project needs to change, I should change it.
But I would like the opportunity to discover those things by actually working on the problem, rather than being told the conclusion before I have started.

sections.heading: Why do we laugh before we understand?
paragraphs: I have been thinking about why people react this way.

Sometimes, I think we are simply uncomfortable with things we cannot immediately understand. If someone proposes an idea that fits neatly into what we already know, we can evaluate it using familiar assumptions. We have seen something similar before. We know what to expect.

But when an idea falls outside that familiar territory, we have to do a little more work. We have to ask questions, imagine possibilities, and consider that our current understanding might not be enough to judge it.
It is easier to laugh.

Calling someone delusional takes less effort than examining their reasoning. Calling something impossible takes less effort than identifying the actual constraints. And telling someone to be realistic can sound like wisdom even when it is simply a way of avoiding a difficult conversation.

Sometimes, the mockery comes from genuine concern. People do not want you to waste money, damage your confidence, or spend months working towards something that may not succeed. That concern can be valid, and I do not want to dismiss it.
Sometimes, it comes from experience. Someone has attempted something similar and knows about difficulties you have not yet encountered. You should listen to that person.
And sometimes, people are just uncomfortable watching someone attempt something they themselves would never dare to try.
I cannot always know which one it is. Neither can you. That is why it is worth listening to criticism without automatically treating it as truth or automatically dismissing it as jealousy.
The important question is not whether people laugh at your idea. It is whether their reasons survive examination.
If they point out a genuine flaw, fix it. If they identify a missing skill, learn it. If they explain a practical constraint, account for it. If the idea still has potential, keep working.
But if all they have is a laugh and a declaration that you are mad, you are not obligated to treat that as a serious evaluation.

And the same goes for the people who call themselves founders. I do not need to laugh at your business simply because it is small. I do not need to mock your startup because it uses existing AI models. I do not need to dismiss your ambition because you are at the beginning.
I can ask what you are building. I can ask why it matters. I can ask whether your product solves a real problem and whether you have evidence that somebody needs it.
Those are fair questions. If you cannot answer them yet, that does not mean you should give up. It means you have more work to do.
Would it not be better if we could have those conversations without making everything a competition over who looks more successful?

sections.heading: Your idea does not need applause. It needs evidence.
paragraphs: Here is something I have had to remind myself of, too.

Being mocked does not automatically mean you are onto something. Just because people do not understand your idea does not make it revolutionary. And being the only person in a room who believes in something does not necessarily make you the smartest person in that room.
Sometimes, you are the only person who has not noticed the obvious problem yet.
So what do you do?

You build a prototype. You speak to the people who might actually use it. You test your assumptions. You estimate the cost. You investigate the alternatives. You learn what already exists. You find out whether the problem is real and whether your proposed solution makes things meaningfully better.

If you are building an AI startup, this means more than making a demo that works beautifully in a carefully prepared video. Can your product handle real users? Does it fail safely? Is it reliable? Does it save people enough time or money to justify its cost? Does it do something meaningfully better than the tools they already have?

If you are building a clothing brand, talk to your customers. Find out what they actually want. Understand why they would buy from you rather than somebody else. If you are building a hardware project, test the components, measure the limitations, and work through the engineering.
Different businesses have different problems. But they all benefit from confronting reality.
You do not need to convince everybody in advance. You need to gather enough evidence to decide what your next step should be.
And sometimes, the evidence will tell you to stop. That is not necessarily failure. It can mean you saved yourself time, money, and effort by discovering the truth early.
Sometimes, it will tell you to change direction. Sometimes, it will show you that your original idea was wrong but that there is a better problem worth solving nearby.
And sometimes, it will give you a reason to continue when everyone else is still unconvinced.
That is the part I find exciting. Not the fantasy of proving everyone wrong, but the possibility of discovering that something you imagined can actually exist.
I do not want to build things simply to silence the people who laughed at me. That would mean allowing their opinions to dictate what I create.
I want to build things because the problems interest me, because the possibilities excite me, and because I want to find out what happens when I stop imagining and start doing.
If the result turns out to be useful, wonderful. If it does not, I hope I have learned enough to make the next attempt better.
And if you have a business, I hope you reach a point where you no longer need to convince people that you are an entrepreneur. The work will speak for itself.

sections.heading: So, what should you actually do with your business?
paragraphs: If you have started a clothing brand, keep going. But ask yourself what you want it to become. Understand your customers. Improve your products. Give people a reason to choose you. Build something beyond a logo and a launch post.

If you have started a jewellery business, learn your market. Understand what your customers value. Pay attention to quality, trust, pricing, and the experience of buying from you. Find the thing you can do exceptionally well.

If you are reselling products, there is still room to build something worthwhile. Perhaps you make discovery easier, curate products for a specific audience, offer a better buying experience, or solve a problem that larger sellers overlook.

If you are building an AI product, please, for the love of everything, think beyond the fact that you have connected a model to an application. Understand the workflow. Build for the people who need it. Make it reliable. Give customers a reason to choose you even when the underlying models improve and your competitors copy your features.
You do not have to change the world. You do have to understand the world your business operates in.
Talk to customers. Learn from competitors. Pay attention to what people actually buy, not just what they compliment. Be honest about what is working and what is not.

And if your original idea is simply that you want to make money, that is an honest place to begin. Just understand that a business requires more than the desire to earn. It requires giving someone a reason to hand you their money in exchange for something they value.
There is no shame in starting small. There is no shame in starting with something ordinary. There is no shame in learning as you go.
The shame, if there is any, lies in becoming so attached to the identity of being a business owner that you stop asking whether the business is actually serving anyone.

Do not be embarrassed that your first idea is simple. Be willing to improve it. Do not be embarrassed that you have competitors. Learn from them. Do not be embarrassed that you are still figuring things out. Everyone who has built anything meaningful had a beginning.

And you do not need to put CEO in your bio to make the beginning count. You do not need to announce that you are disrupting an industry before you have understood it. You do not need to convince the internet that you are important.
Build something. Learn something. Help someone. Repeat.
Just do not confuse beginning with finishing.

sections.heading: And to the people with ideas that sound a little mad...
paragraphs: I want to say something to the person who has an idea they are almost embarrassed to share because they already know what the reaction will be.
The person who has been told to be realistic so many times that they have started questioning whether ambition itself is something to apologise for.
The person who has a notebook full of ideas, a prototype that barely works, or a project that looks ridiculous to everyone who has not taken the time to understand it.
I hope you give yourself permission to try.
Not because every ambitious idea deserves to become a company. Not because the world owes you success. Not because everyone who doubts you is secretly threatened by your potential.
Try because you deserve the opportunity to find out what you are capable of doing.

Learn enough to know what you are attempting. Respect the constraints. Be honest about the risks. Listen to people who know more than you. And be willing to change your mind when the evidence demands it.
But do not abandon an idea solely because someone laughed before you had the chance to explain it.

There is a difference between being ambitious and being careless. There is a difference between believing in yourself and believing you cannot be wrong. There is a difference between ignoring criticism and refusing to let criticism be the only thing that decides your future.
You can be ambitious and humble at the same time. You can dream big and still do the boring work. You can believe something is possible without pretending it is easy.

In fact, I would argue that the people who build meaningful things need all three: imagination to see what could exist, humility to recognise what they do not know, and persistence to keep working when the first attempt fails.
You do not need to prove your idea to the entire world today. Start by proving one small part of it to yourself.

And if you are already calling yourself a founder, a CEO, or the next big thing in AI, I hope you give yourself that same permission to be a beginner. You do not have to pretend you have everything figured out. You do not have to make your business sound bigger than it is.

There is something genuinely respectable about saying, "I am trying to build this. I do not know if it will work yet, but here is the problem I am trying to solve, and here is what I have learned so far."
That is infinitely more interesting to me than another declaration that you are changing the world.
You might actually change something someday. But you have to do the work first.

sections.heading: I am still figuring this out myself.
paragraphs: I want to end this by returning to where I started.
I do not promote my friends’ businesses. I wish them luck. I hope they succeed. I hope they earn money, learn things, find customers, and build something they are proud of.
I am not their judge. I am not the authority on what deserves to exist. I am not sitting on a mountain of successful companies, handing out verdicts to people who are still at the beginning.

I am a guy with ambitions of his own, trying to turn some of them into reality. I know how frustrating it can be when people dismiss an idea without understanding it, and I know how important it is to have the humility to admit that an idea still needs to prove itself.
Both things can be true.
Your business deserves the chance to be built. It does not automatically deserve to succeed. My idea deserves the chance to be tested. It does not automatically deserve to be called innovation.
The world does not owe any of us applause for starting something. We earn trust by doing the work, solving problems, learning from mistakes, and giving people something worth their attention.

So start the clothing brand. Launch the jewellery store. Build the app. Start the AI company. Open the shop. Try the idea you have been thinking about for months. Do the thing you have been too scared to begin.

But once you have started, do not stop asking questions. Do not let the excitement of being an entrepreneur replace the responsibility of building a good business. Do not confuse people congratulating you with people needing what you offer.

And if you are someone with an unconventional idea, do not let the fear of being laughed at stop you from testing it. But do not let your desire to prove people wrong become an excuse to ignore evidence, either.

I am saying all of this while still figuring things out myself. I have no grand success story to sell you. I am not writing this from the finish line. I am somewhere in the middle, trying to build things, questioning my own ideas, and learning to distinguish ambition from delusion.
Maybe some of my ideas will work. Maybe some will fail. Maybe I will look back at this article years from now and laugh at how confidently I wrote about things I was still learning to understand.
Honestly, I hope I do. It would mean I have grown.
But I would rather try, learn, and occasionally embarrass myself than spend my life waiting for permission to begin.

So, no, I do not hate your business. I do not want you to fail. I do not think my ideas are automatically better than yours. And I do not think every person with a CEO title is a fraud or every AI startup is useless.
I just want us to care a little less about looking like entrepreneurs and a little more about becoming people who can actually build something worthwhile.
Start small. Start ordinary. Start with something that already exists, if that is what you know how to do.
Just give people a reason to care beyond the fact that you started.
And if your business turns out to be genuinely useful, different, or simply better at serving the people who need it, I will be happy for you.
I might not promote it. But I will wish you luck.
Because I know what it feels like to be at the beginning of something and have no idea whether it will work.

And if there is one thing I hope people learn when they encounter my own ideas, it is this: question them, challenge them, tell me what is wrong with them. Just give me the courtesy of understanding what I am trying to build before you decide it is impossible.
I can handle being wrong.
I just do not want to be told I am wrong by someone who never bothered to look.
And if you are reading this with CEO, CMO, CTO, Founder, Co-Founder, Visionary, Disruptor, or whatever the fuck else in your bio, please, take a breath.

You do not have to be the next Elon Musk. You do not have to raise millions. You do not have to build a company that changes the world. You do not have to convince strangers on LinkedIn that you are important.
Build something you believe in. Make it useful. Learn from the people who use it. Be honest about what you have achieved and what you have not. Let yourself be a beginner without being ashamed of it.
And if you genuinely build something great, people will have a reason to care. You will not have to keep reminding them of your title.
Until then, maybe spend a little less time updating your bio and a little more time building the thing your bio claims you are building.
Nobody owes your business attention. Nobody owes your startup applause. And nobody owes you admiration simply because you have decided to call yourself a founder.
Give us something worth caring about.
Then we can talk.
Anyway, that is enough ranting from me. I have unfinished projects to work on and absolutely no billion-dollar company to run.
Lmao.

title: How I Use Sarcasm as My Defense Mechanism.
subtitle: I made a personality out of being the funny guy. Now I wonder if I can ever escape it.
excerpt: I joke about everything. People laugh, people judge, and sometimes nobody takes me seriously. But what happens when the personality you built to make people comfortable becomes the very thing that stops them from seeing you?

photoFrame.caption: I AM HIM, HE IS ME.

content.lead: Everyone knows me as the funny guy. The unserious guy. The guy who can turn a perfectly normal conversation into an unnecessary comedy show, who has a sarcastic response ready before you have even finished your sentence, and who apparently considers being serious for more than thirty seconds a personal attack. And honestly? Fair enough. I have given people plenty of reasons to see me that way. But lately, I have been wondering whether I have made being funny such a big part of my personality that people have forgotten there is an actual person behind all the nonsense. Worse, I wonder whether I have made them forget it because, somewhere along the way, I have started forgetting it myself.

sections.heading: The funny guy. That is me, apparently.
paragraphs: If you know me personally, you probably know what I am talking about. I joke around. I tease people. I use sarcasm as though somebody is paying me per sarcastic remark. I can make fun of myself, make fun of you, and somehow find a way to make an ordinary conversation feel like a poorly funded comedy show that nobody asked for.

Sometimes the situation is funny. Sometimes the timing is perfect. Sometimes my brain simply refuses to let a perfectly normal sentence exist without adding something completely unnecessary to it. And sometimes, I genuinely do not know why I said what I said. The words leave my mouth, the damage is done, and only then does my brain arrive at the scene of the crime.

But I genuinely enjoy making people laugh. I like being able to lighten the mood when things get awkward, make a boring conversation entertaining, or give somebody a reason to smile. There is something nice about knowing that your presence can make somebody's day a little better. You do not always need to do something extraordinary for somebody. Sometimes, you just need to make them laugh.

I am not going to sit here and pretend that my entire personality is some elaborate psychological defence mechanism. Sometimes I am happy. Sometimes I am comfortable. Sometimes something is genuinely funny, and I want to laugh about it. There does not need to be a tragic backstory behind every stupid thing I say.
But there is a difference between enjoying humour and becoming so associated with it that people start expecting it from you all the time. And I think that is where things get complicated.
Because somewhere along the way, being funny stopped being just something I did. It became something people expected me to be.
And now I am not entirely sure what happens when I am not.

sections.heading: Congratulations. You have built a personality you cannot escape.
paragraphs: Here is something I find genuinely frustrating. When you are the person who jokes about everything, people start treating your serious moments like they are just another setup for a punchline.

You say something important, and somebody laughs. You try to explain something sincerely, and somebody assumes you are being sarcastic. You express an actual opinion, and suddenly you have to convince people that, for once in your life, you are not messing around.

And what are you supposed to do? Start every conversation with a disclaimer? "Hello, everyone. Before I begin, I would like to clarify that the following statement is sincere and should not be interpreted as a joke. Thank you for your cooperation."

Imagine having to submit an application to be taken seriously. Imagine being asked for supporting documents every time you try to express an actual thought. Apparently, my credibility has been under review for quite some time.

The frustrating part is that I cannot entirely blame people for this. If I have spent so much time joking around, why would they automatically assume that I have suddenly changed my tone? They have become familiar with a version of me that I have repeatedly shown them. They are responding to the person they know.
But that does not make it any less frustrating when I genuinely want to be heard.

And perhaps that is the consequence of building your identity around one particular trait. People begin to associate you with it so strongly that anything outside it feels unusual. You are not just a person who happens to be funny anymore. You are the funny person. That becomes your role in the group, your contribution to a conversation, and sometimes the only thing people seem to expect from you.

If I am quiet, people ask what happened. If I am serious, people ask whether I am okay. If I say something emotional without immediately ruining it with a joke, somebody will probably look at me as though I have just announced that I am leaving the country to become a monk.
Relax. I am still here. Unfortunately for you, I have more jokes.

Except, sometimes, I do not want to make another joke. Sometimes I want to finish a sentence without having to prove that I mean it. Sometimes I want to talk about something that matters to me without feeling the need to make the conversation entertaining for everybody else.
And I wonder whether I have made that unnecessarily difficult for myself.

Because how do you ask people to take a side of you seriously when you have spent so long making sure they associate you with the opposite? How do you complain about being misunderstood when you have trained people to interpret your words as humour? And how do you change that perception without feeling like you are suddenly performing a completely different personality?

I do not have a neat answer to any of these questions. I just know that there are moments when I wish people would listen to what I am actually saying instead of immediately deciding how they are supposed to react to it.
I want to be funny because I find things funny, not because I feel like I have to be funny to justify my presence.
There is a difference. I am still trying to figure out how to live with it.

sections.heading: Why am I like this in the first place?
paragraphs: This is the question I keep coming back to. Why do I joke so much? Why is sarcasm such a natural response for me? Why can I be in the middle of a serious situation and still find something to laugh about, sometimes when I really should not?

Is it simply my personality? Am I naturally like this? Is it a habit I have developed over time? Am I insecure? Do I need people to like me? Do I enjoy being the person who gets a reaction from everybody in the room?
Or am I overthinking something that is not nearly as complicated as I am making it sound?

Honestly, I do not know. And I do not want to manufacture some dramatic explanation just to make this article sound profound. I am not a psychologist, and I cannot diagnose my entire personality by staring at it long enough. Sometimes I am just a twenty-year-old trying to understand why his mouth operates without adult supervision.

But I do think insecurity is worth considering. Not because I have concluded that I am secretly insecure about everything, but because I think it is worth asking why certain behaviours become so important to us.

Do I enjoy making people laugh simply because laughter feels good? Or is there a part of me that enjoys knowing I can make people like having me around? Is there a difference between wanting to make somebody happy and wanting to be the person responsible for making them happy?
Perhaps there is. Perhaps there is not.

I wonder whether being funny gives me a certain amount of comfort in social situations. If I can make people laugh, the interaction feels successful. There is a reaction. There is a connection. I know what to do next. I do not have to sit there wondering whether the other person is bored, whether I am saying the wrong thing, or whether the conversation is dying a slow and painful death.

Humour gives you something to contribute. It gives you a way to enter a conversation, keep it going, and make yourself memorable. And when people respond positively, it feels good. Who does not enjoy being appreciated?

But what happens when that appreciation becomes something you start depending on? What happens when you feel like you need to be entertaining because you are no longer sure what else you bring to the table?
That is a much less comfortable question.

Maybe I am not insecure. Maybe I just enjoy humour. Maybe both things can be true. Maybe I am confident enough to be ridiculous, but still uncertain about how people will respond when I stop being ridiculous. Maybe I have never really thought about the distinction until now.

I do not want to turn every part of my personality into a symptom. Being funny is not a disease. Being playful is not a character flaw. And there is nothing wrong with wanting people to enjoy your company.
But if I am honest with myself, I should at least be willing to ask whether I sometimes use humour to avoid the discomfort of being seen without it.
Because that is the thing about self-reflection. You do not always discover something flattering. Sometimes you just find another question you would rather make a joke about.
Which, coincidentally, is exactly what I am trying not to do right now.

sections.heading: Sarcasm is convenient. Sometimes a little too convenient.
paragraphs: Let us talk about sarcasm itself, because I think it deserves some of the blame here. Not all of it, obviously. I am still responsible for the nonsense coming out of my own mouth. But sarcasm can be an incredibly convenient way of communicating without having to communicate properly.

You can say something serious and make it sound unserious. You can express an opinion without having to stand completely behind the vulnerability of expressing it. You can tell somebody something that matters to you and, if the response makes you uncomfortable, immediately retreat into the familiar territory of "Bro, I was joking."
It is a brilliant little escape route. A terrible communication strategy, perhaps, but a brilliant escape route.

Imagine telling somebody that you miss them, then immediately adding something sarcastic so the conversation does not become too emotional. Imagine being hurt by something someone said but responding with a joke because admitting that it affected you feels unnecessarily uncomfortable. Imagine wanting to tell somebody that you care about them, but finding it easier to annoy them for twenty minutes instead.

Now, I am not claiming that I do all these things in every relationship or that every sarcastic person is secretly hiding some enormous emotional wound. That would be a ridiculous generalisation. Sometimes a joke is just a joke. Sometimes people are simply being playful, and we should be allowed to enjoy that without turning it into a three-hour therapy session.
But humour can make difficult things easier to approach. It can also make them easier to avoid.
And perhaps that is the contradiction. A joke can help you say something you would otherwise struggle to say, but it can also give you an excuse not to acknowledge that you meant it.

You can hide a serious thought inside a funny sentence. If the other person understands, wonderful. If they do not, you can pretend it was never serious in the first place. You get to test the waters without fully stepping into them.

Except that sometimes the other person does not understand. Sometimes they laugh at the very thing you were trying to communicate sincerely. Sometimes you make a joke when what you actually wanted was to be understood, and the moment passes before you have the courage to try again.
And sometimes you do not even realise that was what you wanted until much later.
I wonder how often we make ourselves difficult to understand and then become frustrated when people misunderstand us.

That question is uncomfortable because it removes the convenience of blaming everybody else. It asks whether I have ever expected somebody to understand a part of me that I have never properly shown them.

Have I ever wanted someone to recognise that I was serious without actually behaving seriously? Have I expected people to read between the lines while giving them every possible reason to believe there were no lines to read?
Perhaps.

I can say that my humour is part of who I am, and I genuinely believe that. But if I use it every time a conversation becomes uncomfortable, then it stops being only a way of expressing myself. It becomes a way of controlling how much of myself I allow other people to see.

I do not know whether I do that deliberately. I suspect that a lot of habits begin without us making a conscious decision to develop them. We repeat something because it works, then keep repeating it until we no longer question why we do it.
Maybe sarcasm has simply become the easiest response available to me. Maybe I have practised being funny so often that I reach for humour before I have even worked out what I actually want to say.
And maybe learning to be sincere sometimes means allowing a moment to remain uncomfortable instead of immediately trying to rescue it with a punchline.
Disgusting concept. Horrible. Absolutely unacceptable.
I am going to need some time to process that.

sections.heading: Depending on who you are, you get a different me.
paragraphs: Here is another thing about me that I find difficult to explain without making it sound like I have several personalities competing for custody of my body.

Around my parents, I can be a kid. Around relatives, I can be the quietest person in the room, barely speaking unless I actually have something to say. Around my friends, I can turn into a completely different creature. A wild animal, if you will. A public nuisance with internet access.
And if you have seen all three versions, congratulations. You have unlocked the full character pack.

I do not know how else to explain it. I behave differently depending on who I am with. My energy changes. The way I speak changes. The amount of nonsense I am willing to say out loud changes dramatically.
Idk. That is just me, depending on you.

And I do not necessarily think that is a bad thing. We all behave differently around different people. Most of us are not going to interact with a close friend the same way we interact with a stranger, a professor, a relative, or our parents. Relationships have different boundaries, different histories, and different levels of comfort.

There are people around whom I feel comfortable being completely ridiculous. There are people around whom I prefer to listen. There are people with whom I can talk about things that matter to me, and there are people with whom I simply do not feel the need to say much at all.
That does not automatically make any of those versions fake. They are all parts of me that emerge in different environments.
But it does make me wonder how much of our personality is something we bring into a room and how much of it is something that comes out because of the people already in it.

Am I naturally loud, or am I loud around people who make me feel comfortable? Am I naturally quiet, or do certain environments make me feel like there is no point in speaking? Am I always this sarcastic, or does the people around me influence how much of that side I show?
Perhaps it is a combination of all of them.

There is a line I keep coming back to: I am the way I show myself to you. If I joke around with you, tease you, and make an effort to keep the conversation going, that is genuinely how I am choosing to interact with you. I am not necessarily pretending to be somebody else.

But I also think people bring something out of us. When somebody is kind to me, when I feel accepted rather than judged, I find it easier to relax. I can be stupid without worrying about every little thing I say. I can let a conversation go wherever it wants to go. I do not have to calculate every interaction.
I can just exist.

And I think there is something quite nice about that. Being around someone who makes you feel like you do not have to constantly edit yourself is a privilege. It is a kind of comfort that does not always need to be announced.

At the same time, comfort does not excuse everything. Just because I feel comfortable joking with somebody does not mean they are comfortable being the target of every joke. Just because I know I mean well does not mean the other person will experience it that way.
I can be myself and still be wrong. I can have good intentions and still hurt somebody. I can genuinely care about a person and still fail to communicate that care in a way they understand.
Being yourself is not a free pass to disregard how you affect other people.
I want to hold on to the freedom of being comfortable around people without turning that freedom into an excuse to stop paying attention to them.
And yes, that applies even when I am being funny. Especially then.

sections.heading: Not everyone gets the same version of me. And that is okay.
paragraphs: I would also be lying if I pretended that I am equally warm, friendly, and interested in everybody. I am not.

There are people I naturally get along with, people I respect but do not particularly connect with, and people whose company I would rather avoid. Some conversations come naturally to me. Others feel like I am trying to start a car that has been sitting in the rain for seventeen years.

If I am comfortable around you, you will probably see my humour, my enthusiasm, and my willingness to engage. If I am not, I may be quieter, more distant, or considerably less interested in keeping the conversation alive.

And yes, I can be blunt. I can be rude. I can become sarcastic in a way that is considerably less friendly than the version people usually experience. I have flaws. I am not writing this article to disguise them as charming personality traits.

Sometimes, I genuinely do not like somebody. Sometimes our personalities do not match. Sometimes I do not agree with the way someone behaves, and I do not feel any particular desire to become close to them.
I do not think I owe everybody friendship, constant attention, or access to my personal life. I do not think I need to become universally likeable to be a decent person.

But there is a difference between not liking somebody and believing you have the right to treat them badly. I can keep my distance without humiliating someone. I can disagree without turning every conversation into a personal attack. I can decide that somebody is not my kind of person without making it my mission to make them feel small.
I do not always get that right. I am aware of that.

And perhaps that is another thing I need to learn: being unapologetically yourself does not mean being unwilling to examine yourself. There is a difference between accepting your personality and defending every single thing you do in its name.

I can accept that sarcasm is part of me while acknowledging that sometimes I use it badly. I can accept that I am not going to connect with everybody while still treating people with basic decency. I can refuse to change myself just to satisfy everyone and still change the parts of myself that genuinely need work.
Those things can exist together.
I do not want to become a person who apologises for every little thing that makes him different. But I also do not want to become a person who thinks being different means he never has to apologise.

sections.heading: What happens when people stop taking you seriously?
paragraphs: I think this is the part that bothers me more than I usually admit.

It is one thing for somebody to think you are funny. It is another for them to assume that being funny is all you are capable of. It is one thing for people to enjoy your jokes. It is another for them to stop listening when you are no longer making one.

Because I do have serious thoughts. I do think about things. I care about certain subjects, certain people, and certain questions about life more than my everyday behaviour might suggest. I can spend hours thinking about something that matters to me, write about it, argue about it, and try to understand it from different perspectives.

I can think about human suffering, relationships, faith, ambition, insecurity, and the kind of person I want to become. I can take the future seriously. I can care about what is happening around me. I can have opinions that I have genuinely thought through.
And then I can go right back to sending the most brain-dead message imaginable.
Both things are true. I do not see why they should contradict each other.

But I sometimes wonder whether people who know me primarily through my humour ever see that other side. And if they do not, is it because they have chosen not to look, or because I have never really given them a reason to?
Perhaps I have made myself easy to underestimate.

That is a difficult thing to admit because it is tempting to make the entire problem somebody else's fault. It is tempting to say that people are shallow, that they judge too quickly, that they cannot look beyond a first impression. And sometimes, that might genuinely be true.
